entries.title: In Contentious Takoma Park Race, Civility Is a Campaign Issue
entries.summary: The mayor told a resident to show “respect” and be quiet during a council meeting. Now he’s running against her.
entries.content:
It was two hours into a Takoma Park City Council meeting, and the mayor wasn’t tolerating interruptions.

“I just ask you to respect our panelists and the people that are here, and to not disrupt this meeting,” first-term Mayor Talisha Searcy said firmly during the 2023 exchange with Tom Gagliardo, an attorney who had — unprompted — shouted an opinion about a city planning matter.

When Gagliardo asked permission to speak, Searcy told him, “No, sir, you cannot,” noting that it wasn’t the public comment period. He complied, but with a parting shot: “Just don’t diss anybody else.”

Nobody knew then that, three years later, Gagliardo, 79, a former Takoma Park city attorney, would be running to unseat Searcy, 46 — and that decorum and civility would become a campaign issue after Searcy ordered an end to clapping and booing to retain order during another meeting last February.

“Clap-gate,” Searcy jokingly calls the flap that Gagliardo has turned into a campaign issue ahead of the Nov. 3 election in the Montgomery County city of 17,000 that borders Washington. (Because the mayoral elections are nonpartisan, so there was no primary.)

Progressive, quirky Takoma Park, a town of old bungalows and mature trees nicknamed “The People’s Republic of Takoma Park” and “Granola Park,” has long charted a unique course in emphasizing citizen participation in government. It allows non-U.S. citizens and 16-year-olds to vote in city elections. The environmentally conscious citizens’ center is named for a former activist and mayor who once stood in front of a bulldozer to block a highway and helped make the city an official sanctuary for political refugees.

But free speech doesn’t mean applauding during council meetings or shouting down political rivals, says Searcy, a federal government health policy official and former city council member. She notes that even the sharply divided Congress doesn’t permit outbursts during committee hearings.
IMG_1925 copy.jpg (6151x4032, AR: 1.53)“One of the things that my opponent doesn’t necessarily understand is that asking you to comply with the rules of order does not mean that you’re taking away someone’s freedom of speech,” she said in an interview. “In meetings following the [February] meeting, there were residents that stated they don’t like to speak at council meetings because of the behavior.”

The February meeting was marked by applause, cursing and outbursts during discussion of the city’s rent stabilization laws. One man raised a middle finger at the lawmakers after a profanity-filled speech at the microphone.

“What I witnessed this evening was blatant disrespect of me in my role as the presiding officer [and] blatant disrespect for others in this room,” Searcy said at the meeting, carefully measuring her words and pausing occasionally to collect herself.

She lamented “an environment where disrespect breeds disrespect” and where “somebody feels empowered to flip us off.”

Terry Seamens, a former council member supporting Searcy, said Gagliardo has often attended council meetings with several others, and the group “just kind of heckled people or made comments, or guffaws or boos when people were talking, and the mayor tried to stop that.”

Gagliardo, a white-haired labor and employment lawyer, said in an interview that he supports orderly meetings, but “you either value public input, whether supportive or critical, or you don't. I do. The incumbent doesn't. That's one reason why I'm running.”

Gagliardo, during a recent meet-and-greet session, sat in an armchair in a resident’s living room on a quiet, tree-lined street and told a dozen voters of his concerns with the clapping restriction in addition to a proposal endorsed by Searcy to study holding city elections every four years instead of every two.

Searcy says holding elections less frequently could save the city money and cut down on time lawmakers spend campaigning rather than legislating. Gagliardo says the change would make elected officials less accountable.

“You know, some people might say, ‘Well they’re not really that important,” Gagliardo said of the two issues, but added: “I think a lot of people are going to vote based on this.”

The volatile February meeting touched on a city-commissioned study examining possible changes to Takoma Park’s program limiting how much landlords can increase rents.
DC0A7408 copy.jpg (5840x3893, AR: 1.50)Rent control changes are sensitive topics in Takoma Park, where increasing affluence has brought higher housing costs and concerns that longtime renters, including members of large immigrant communities, could be priced out.

“Takoma Park is a diverse community. It's got many single-family homes, but it also has many multifamily homes,” said Jim Douglas of Historic Takoma, a heritage preservation group. “It has a variety of income levels and certainly a variety of races and ethnicities.”

Searcy and Gagliardo both emphasize preserving that diversity. Their race can be seen as a competition to out-Takoma-Park each other by championing the progressive, multicultural values that have long defined a city known for farmers markets with an international flavor, and a colorful Fourth of July parade lampooning politicians (mostly Republicans) with whom it disagrees.

In campaign appearances, Gagliardo has taken aim at proposals backed by Searcy to explore rent control changes, including lengthening the amount of time — currently five years — landlords are exempt from rent increase rules after a new property opens.

“She wants to triple the length of time that new construction is exempt,” Gagliardo said. “I don’t.”

Searcy said she hasn’t settled on how long an exemption period should be. But she questions whether the five-year waiver for newly constructed units provides potential developers enough revenue to recoup their initial investment and encourages new construction. Montgomery County’s exemption, which Takoma Park is not bound by, is 23 years.

“I’ve said, ‘Hey, I don’t know yet,’” Searcy said. “I know five is too short.”

Searcy said her general leadership style is to seek consensus if possible and listen to opposing views.

While she said she doesn’t like name-calling in politics, she emphasizes that she can take it.

“I have thick skin. My first job was at a Waffle House,” she said. “I’ve heard and seen it all.”

entries.title: Back to Business
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 15, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: The D.C. Council’s return, a rent-inflation settlement and the DMV’s worst drivers. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit: 10/10. Wall-to-wall sunshine, refreshingly dry air and highs from the mid-70s to around 80 — about as perfect as a September day gets. Read the full forecast.

THE LATEST

Summer break is over for the D.C. Council.

City lawmakers are back this week from their two-month summer recess, and they’ve got a busy fall ahead of them. It’s the tail end of their two-year legislative cycle, so council members will be rushing to pass their preferred bills into law. That’s even more the case this time as there will be a big turnover come January, with four current lawmakers headed for the exit — one of them, Janeese Lewis George, presumably to serve as mayor.

The city’s shaky finances will be top of mind. In mid-October, the council will host a roundtable on possible tax increases and other revenue raisers. A New York City-style pied-à-terre tax is on the agenda, as is a capital gains tax increase for wealthy households. It remains to be seen whether anything moves beyond the idea stage, though.

Waymo will be getting way more attention, too. The council is expected to debate a bill that would legalize passenger service in self-driving cars, and the fight is likely to be intense. Labor unions are against Waymo and its ilk coming to D.C., and even Uber — a later entrant in the autonomous vehicle market — is pushing to slow-roll the measure. Lewis George herself has been a self-driving skeptic, but Waymo is hoping to neutralize her with a hiring and charm offensive.

How many publicly funded stadiums is too many? That’s a question council members will have to answer as they consider a bill that would put $300 million in taxpayer money toward adding 8,000 seats and a roof to Audi Field. Mayor Muriel Bowser — who championed public money for a new Commanders stadium — is opposed, saying the larger soccer stadium would cannibalize Capital One Arena, which is also being renovated with city funds. Relatedly, the council will be asked to sign off on the master plan for the residential and retail development around the new Commanders stadium.

Speaking of Bowser, the outgoing mayor is pushing the council to take further steps to make D.C. more attractive for private investment in the housing market. To that end, she wants lawmakers to make it easier for landlords to evict tenants and give squatters the boot. A public hearing on improving housing conditions is also on the agenda.

A legacy is also on the mind of Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau, who will be pushing her colleagues to sign off on her bill that would introduce a refundable 10-cent deposit for bottles and cans. She says it would reduce litter, but critics say it would increase costs for cash-strapped local businesses.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Two D.C. landlords will pay $9.3 million to resolve claims that they “illegally conspired” to inflate rents across the thousands of apartments they own across the city, The Washington Sun’s Zara Norman reports. It’s the biggest settlement to date in an ongoing series of suits between the D.C. attorney general’s office and 14 local landlords accused of using RealPage software to inflate rental prices at tens of thousands of apartments across the District, which allegedly resulted in renters paying millions of dollars more than they should have.

The Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s bid to restrict and change the process for mailing ballots ahead of November’s midterm elections, The Sun’s Adora Brown and Gavin J. Quinton report. The decision clears the way for states to stick with their processes and prevents a major headache for election officials in D.C., where every registered voter receives a ballot in the mail.

Arrests by U.S. Park Police have nearly doubled in the past year, while the number of park police officers working in and around D.C. has more than doubled, City Cast D.C. reports.

The Commanders and D.C. have unveiled the designs of two parking garages that will be built alongside the new stadium at the old RFK site. The two decks are expected to hold up to 6,000 cars, but earlier this year federal regulators expressed concern that large structures would interfere with views of the stadium.

Pressure is mounting on D.C. to explain how it has been using Flock license-plate readers, and now council member Brooke Pinto, who chairs the council committee that oversees the police, is asking interim Chief Jeffery Carroll for more details. “The public deserves transparency and must understand how this technology is being used in our communities,” she said in a public letter to the police department.






FROM MARYLAND

Takoma Park’s mayor told a resident to show “respect” and be quiet during a council meeting. Now he’s running against her in an unusually combative race, Jeff Barker reports for The Sun.





FROM THE ROAD

Are Maryland drivers really the worst? Nearly half of those who answered The Sun’s poll last week said yes. And elsewhere on the internet, Reddit declared that the driver who crashed through a U-Haul facility in Navy Yard this weekend must have hailed from Maryland.

The Sun’s Andrew Van Dam reports that, at first glance, the data seems to confirm that enduring DMV stereotype: From 2019 to 2021, Maryland drivers were at fault in more two-car crashes in D.C. than drivers from anywhere else, including D.C.

But, wait! There’s more! Maryland drivers are overrepresented. Of D.C. workers who commute by car, 48% drove in from Maryland between 2022 and 2024. Those drivers are only slightly more likely to be at fault in an accident as they are to be innocent victims, according The Sun’s analysis of about a decade of police data ending in 2021.

The real culprit? Virginians, who were 20% more likely to be at fault.

DCdrivers online notus-03.png (3034x945, AR: 3.21)


SPORTS

Look who's back. Alex Ovechkin returned to the ice with the Capitals on Monday. A few days after flying back to D.C. for his 22nd season, Ovi participated in 45 minutes of scrimmaging during an informal skate at the Caps' practice rink in Arlington, The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri reports. It was his first time sharing the ice with a number of new teammates, including offseason acquisitions Jordan Kyrou, Alex Tuch and Boone Jenner. Training camp starts Thursday, which is also Ovechkin's 41st birthday.

What did the Commanders learn in Philadelphia? The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson looks at the good and the bad from Sunday’s season-opening loss to the Eagles. One glaring issue? Washington had trouble getting Terry McLaurin the ball. That will have to change if the Commanders are going to take advantage of Dallas’ seemingly spotty defense on Sunday.

The Spirit’s scoring woes continued Sunday, as Washington was shut out for the third time in its last five home games. The match against Boston Legacy FC presented a prime opportunity for the Spirit to maintain momentum against one of the NWSL’s weaker teams, Nicky Wolcott writes for The Sun. Instead, Washington generated few real chances and gave up a barrage of late goals in a stunning 3-0 defeat. The Spirit remains in second place in the league table, but will surely have to pick up its offense to remain in real contention.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Phillies, 6:45 p.m. (MLB.TV)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Finally, yesterday’s trivia answer was B) The Ramones. Their song “Bad Brain” served as inspiration for the name of legendary D.C. punk group Bad Brains. A special shout-out to Eric Kulberg, who answered first.

entries.title: Don’t Worry, Be Happy With AI
entries.content:
Today’s notice: No one can decide what constitutes being paranoid about AI. Mitch McConnell, back at work. The legal battles against Trump’s political enemies. The national Democratic Party backs more House candidates. And: Christians argue with each other in Washington state.





THE LATEST

Are you too afraid of humanity’s end? Members of Congress scrambled to respond to the wild AI news cycle, which has seen the major corporations building the advanced tech warn that they might have forgotten to carry the seven and inadvertently created a doomsday device — while at the same time moving ahead with plans to raise billions from investors to build more advanced stuff that could also annihilate civilization.

As we told you, betting against short-term congressional action is probably safe. The Washington Sun’s Igor Bobic reported on a day where many lawmakers warned that people were maybe a little too scared and should chill out. Donald Trump led the pack with a post dismissing the fears of AI as a “hoax.” Congressional leaders fell largely in line shortly after. Speaker Mike Johnson cautioned against government regulation as a mere “reflex of legislative bodies” that could stifle innovation and let China lap America in the AI race. (One assumes this is a version of the AI race that ends with humanity not getting turned into batteries à la “The Matrix.”)

Over in the Senate, Republican leader John Thune said he saw this coming back in 2023 and promised to revise his old AI legislation. But he too called for a “light touch” so as not to get in the way of AI’s aspiring growth.

A plan to thread that needle remained largely out of sight yesterday. “We’ve got to absolutely be certain that we’re not doing something to blow our own legs off. I mean, that would be pretty dumb-bunny stuff to me,” Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia) told The Sun’s Manuela Silva. “But there’s so much being afraid of the dark. I’m not afraid of the dark.”

Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) offered his solution: a law requiring a kill switch on AI models. Such a move could “hopefully calm some of the hysteria,” but he acknowledged there may not be enough active concern in Washington to pass even that. “I don’t know how the White House is going to feel about it,” Kennedy said.

Democrats also haven’t decided how scared they should be. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) has introduced a bill to ban AI superintelligence. So far, it has no Democratic co-sponsors.

More: Whistleblower Says DHS’s Hunt for Unlawful Voting May Have Broken State Laws • Thune’s Texas PAC Drops a Whopping $54 Million for Paxton’s Senate Race •  Newsom Says He Won’t Challenge Harris if She Runs in 2028 • Democratic Congressional Candidate Defends Resurfaced Explicit Photos

Open tabs:

  • Why a lawyer who launched the Christian legal movement believes it’s gone astray (WaPo)
  • Inside the US Treasury secretary’s tense relationship with financial media (Semafor)
  • Trump nominates Lee Greenwood’s wife to serve as ambassador to Barbados (CBS)




FROM THE COURTS


Mail-in ballot changes halted: Last night the Supreme Court ended Trump’s push to overhaul and restrict mail-in balloting, allowing state election officials to proceed with their original plans for ballot-handling, The Sun’s Adora Brown and Gavin J. Quinton report. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump appointee, wrote a concurring opinion in the majority, while conservatives appointed by other presidents, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, dissented. The ruling has the potential to be a big setback for the White House’s plans to put more federal control over mail-in balloting. Democrats were quick to applaud it. “Trump, you lost another one,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said.

FROM THE HILL


Return of Mitch McConnell: The elder Republican senator from Kentucky was back at work yesterday after a roughly three-month absence, The Sun’s Reese Gorman reports. “I’m still not quite back to 100%, but I’ve assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me,” a post from McConnell on X read.

FROM THE DOJ


Never-ending criminal investigations: There are “multiple ‘viable’ grand jury investigations” into Trump’s political enemies underway, according to the subject of one of the targets. The lawyer for former CIA Director John Brennan says a Trump official admitted to a number of “far-reaching” cases to probe “issues at Mar-a-Lago and beyond,” The Sun’s Jose Pagliery reports. Kenneth Wainstein, Brennan’s attorney, submitted the revelation in a filing asking a federal judge to force the Trump administration to keep all documents related to Brennan’s ongoing prosecution.

And who from Trumpworld is running point? None other than Kurt Olsen, a MAGA loyalist who helped Trump challenge 2020 election results with debunked conspiracy theories.

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


Democrats expand their House target list: The DCCC added three new candidates to its Red to Blue spending program this morning, including William Lawrence in Michigan who upset the establishment in the primary and has struggled to distance himself from his far-left past.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Small town Christian divide: The deep political divisions among Americans — and the fears that go with them — pop up in the unlikeliest of places. The Sun’s Ellie Silverman reports from the outwardly homogeneous town of Battle Ground, Washington, where Christians are fracturing over what “Christian nationalism” means and the growing local power of a family and a company with ties to the movement.



More: Trump Scraps Biden-Era Climate Pollution Rules for Power Plants • Judge Blocks Trump Rule Limiting Student Visas to Four Years • Trump Eyes World War II Memorial as Next Makeover Project • Kennedy Center Board Lists 10 Options for Putting Trump’s Name on the Building





NOT US

  • Oil Executives Say the Great Fuel Crisis Is Here, by Benoît Morenne and Collin Eaton for The Wall Street Journal
  • Crypto campaign cash could come at a cost for Democrats, by Jasper Goodman for Politico
  • Are hotels people too? In this Delaware town, local businesses can cast ballots. By Dion Nissenbaum for Votebeat




Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of The Washington Sun Newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If this newsletter was shared with you, please sign up — it’s free! Have a tip? Email us at tips@washsun.com. And as always, we’d love to hear your thoughts at newsletters@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Thomas Burr and Andrew Burton.

entries.title: Commanders All-22: What Went Wrong in Washington’s Week 1 Loss
entries.summary: Taking a closer look at all the trips, falls and mistakes from a 24-22 loss to the Eagles.
entries.content:
There’s a lot that went wrong for the Commanders on Sunday in their 24-22 loss to the Eagles. Drops, trips and mental mistakes set Washington up for failure long before the team’s much-discussed two-point conversion attempt in the game’s final moments.

Here’s a closer look at Sunday’s season opener, with some thoughts from the game footage and coach Dan Quinn’s Monday afternoon press conference:

The blocking failed on the two-point conversion.

A lot has been said about the Commanders’ failed shovel pass to tight end John Bates on the two-point conversion at the end of the fourth quarter. But Quinn believes the play was sound, it just wasn’t executed as intended.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“I thought it was a good play,” he said. “It was one that we had practiced, and I thought their player also made a good play spinning out of the block with Nick [Allegretti] to stuff the play to go. I think we really got a great chance to go execute the two-point play.”

At the start of the play, right guard Sam Cosmi pulled left to serve as Bates’ lead blocker. Left guard Chris Paul simultaneously passed off defensive tackle Jalen Carter to left tackle Brandon Coleman. He and Cosmi were supposed to serve as bodyguards leading the way for Bates.

Daniels made edge rusher Jalyx Hunt bite on his fake scramble, which freed up a lane. But defensive tackle Moro Ojomo spun off Allegretti’s block, allowing him to stuff Bates near the line of scrimmage. Even if Allegretti had held his block, there’s no guarantee for success: Paul let his assignment, linebacker Jihaad Campbell, get past him as well.

Dontayvion Wicks’ 64-yard reception was caused by a misunderstanding.

The Eagles’ new wide receiver ran a deep corner route with tight end Dallas Goedert running an out route underneath. Running alongside Wicks, cornerback Mike Sainristil peeked back at Goedert, who was sprinting free after linebacker Frankie Luvu passed him off in zone coverage. Sainristil said after the game that he assumed the ball had gone underneath and so he left Wicks alone to pursue. Seconds later, the ball sailed over Sainristil’s head into the waiting hands of Wicks.

“It wasn't schematically related to him, communication error or normal things that go into a big play,” Quinn said of Sainristil. “So that's definitely the things we will identify with him, and I'm certain that he'll work on that.”

https://x.com/NFLonFOX/status/2099240337474486427
The Eagles worked hard to limit Terry McLaurin.


McLaurin, Washington’s lead receiver since 2019, had just two receptions on four targets Sunday. Quinn said Monday that it’s clear the Eagles tried to limit the wideout’s explosive plays.



“Part of their game plan was to say, ‘This is the person that we want to prevent from the deep balls down the field,’” Quinn said.



With McLaurin blanketed, the Commanders tried to take what they were given. One example from the first drive of the game: McLaurin lined up wide left, his cornerback bumped him at the line and a safety provided overhead coverage. With his top target struggling to find space, Jayden Daniels instead completed a 13-yard pass to Stefon Diggs on an in route.



Later in the game, McLaurin lined up on the right side with the cornerback in press coverage. McLaurin got off the line and built a foot of separation, but his post route ran right into the single-high safety. Daniels instead threw the ball out of bounds, intended for Rachaad White. The Commanders need to find ways to get McLaurin involved if they’re going to find an offensive rhythm this season.


Bad alignment led to Goedert’s second-quarter touchdown.

Quinn said the defense was in Cover 2 on this play, which requires the two safeties to play back while the other defenders manage everything underneath. Safeties Nick Cross and Quan Martin were back while Jeremy Reaves patrolled the middle underneath.

But with the Eagles running four vertical routes, Quinn said the middle of the field was left vulnerable. Goedert found space between Reaves and Martin to bring in the tight throw by Hurts.

https://x.com/NFL/status/2099242632262422940
In an ideal world, there would have been less of a gap between Reaves and Martin, although the Commanders had an identical issue on the other side with Eagles receiver Makai Lemon running free up the seam.

“In that down and distance you'd like to see us align differently where we could maneuver our guys into the right locations to go,” Quinn said.

With a trip to Dallas on Sunday, Washington will need to shore up its coverage plan to handle star wide receivers CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens.

Missed tackles led to Saquon Barkley’s 42-yard run.


On this key second-quarter play, the Eagles offensive line zone blocked to the right, which gave blitzing cornerback Amik Robertson a free lane to the Hurts-Barkley run option exchange. Robertson targeted Hurts, who then released the ball to Barkley, which made Robertson stumble and miss the tackle.



https://x.com/NFLonFOX/status/2099248388734587192



As Barkley hit the hole, Leo Chenal was there to make the stop but got pushed out of position and collided with Robertson. Sainristil was the next defender to meet Barkley, but the running back’s juke move left him behind. Barkley then stepped through Quan Martin’s shoestring tackle to turn a solid run into a big gain.


Jalen Hurts’ 22-yard scramble on third down was aided by two falls. 

The Commanders had two down linemen (Charles Omenihu and Daron Payne) and two edge rushers (Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson) on the line of scrimmage. Omenihu appeared to trip over the foot of Eagles center Cam Jurgens and Payne hit the dirt as well after Jurgens pushed him back.

Linebackers Jordan Magee and Sonny Styles, who initially showed blitz, both dropped into coverage, which left the middle of the field wide open for Hurts.

entries.title: When Accusations of Christian Nationalism Tear a Small Town Apart
entries.summary: In Battle Ground, Washington, neighbors are grappling with an alleged takeover by a local company. One pastor is trying to keep his community together.
entries.content:
BATTLE GROUND, Wash. — Pastor David Lindner glanced over his piano at the congregants taking their seats. He knew there wouldn’t be many, but he told himself that was OK. Smaller was better for talking, and talking was what this town needed.

“Good evening, everybody," Lindner said.

The animosity of national politics had contaminated his small city in the foothills of the Cascade Mountains. City Council meetings deteriorated from discussions of roundabouts, road repairs and pickleball courts to arguments about ICE, anti-fascism, prayer at public meetings and the definition of nuclear families.

Now, people were hurling accusations that Christian nationalists were taking over Main Street.

All this, in a town called Battle Ground.

Lindner, 47, didn’t know what to think, and he didn’t know where everyone in his church stood. Many said they didn’t know what Christian nationalism meant. Lindner wasn’t sure he knew either. But he saw people — his community — fighting and felt called to do something about it.

Across the country, Christian nationalism has swept into mainstream Republican politics, seeking to center Christianity more firmly in civic life. But neighbors ultimately have to wrestle with what that means. Where does proudly practicing Christianity end and Christian nationalism begin? Do the Commandments become law? Do Christians impose their values on non-Christians? And when the backlash comes, who gets caught in it?

For 13 years, Lindner has been the pastor at SixEight, a church named for the Bible verse Micah 6:8, which asks people to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly.

He didn’t talk politics from the pulpit, but if asked, he told the truth. He was raised to support conservative candidates and voted twice for Donald Trump, with reservations. But he didn’t vote for any candidate in the last presidential election. As a part-time choir teacher and drama coach at the local high school, he comforted students who struggled to reconcile their sexuality with their love for Jesus. He told them, “We have no concept of how infinite God's love is.”

Lindner’s church, located a block off the town’s main street, rented its parking lot to the suspected Christian nationalists. His church needed the money, but around town, people balked.

“As a Christian I want to encourage you to reconsider,” one person wrote on Facebook. “Taking their money is tacit approval of their actions, esp to a world hurt by Christians.”
08302026_BattleGround_Church.jpg (4848x3000, AR: 1.62)On this Sunday night in August, Lindner turned to the Didache, a Christian document known to many as the Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, written almost 2,000 years ago.

“What stands out to you?” he asked the people seated at round tables instead of pews, a trick to make the room look less empty. “Anything that surprised you?”

His four children and the rest of the congregation stared back. His wife, Bekki, was the first to call out: “You talked about how we belong to one another.”

“Yeah, we’re not just attending a group meeting together,” he said. “We have a responsibility to one another.”

* * *

Divisive political arguments used to feel far away here, in the shadow of Mount St. Helens.

In a town of almost 24,000, about 85 percent of whom are white, diversity mainly meant a variety of Christians — Catholics, Baptists, Episcopalians, United Methodists, Old Apostolic Lutherans, Presbyterians, Quakers and Evangelicals. There were more than 20 churches. The nearest mosque was 12 miles away.

The town was united in a basic belief in Jesus. A local coffee shop sold a pink guided prayer journal titled “This Mama Prays.” A boutique sold cross necklaces and a sweatshirt that said “SAVED.”

But this year, something changed. People started claiming that a local company, Maddox Industrial Transformer, and anyone associated with the people running it, were Christian nationalists.
08302026_BattleGround_001 copy.jpg (3000x4867, AR: 0.62)Those claims targeted the brothers who run Maddox, Camden and Mac Spiller; their pastor, C.R. Wiley; the town’s mayor, who works at the company; and several local businesses the brothers invested in, such as the farmer’s market, the bakery and the newspaper. 

Camden Spiller said in an email to The Washington Sun that he does not identify as a Christian nationalist. Mac Spiller, Wiley and Mayor Eric Overholser did not respond to interview requests.

Now, across town, people were taking sides.

Over July Fourth weekend, thousands gathered near the Maddox headquarters as fireworks exploded across the Pacific Northwest sky.

Kids ate free hot dogs and played in the bounce house. They had their faces painted and decorated tricycles for a parade. Balloons were twisted into animals and swords. Betsy Ross mingled in the crowd.

But plenty of other people had started seeing any gesture from Maddox as nefarious.

So as soon as the Rev. Kate Lore, a retired ordained Unitarian Universalist minister, heard about the free event, sponsored by Maddox, she thought:

“It's part of the Trojan horse.”

* * *

Lindner used to watch Sean Hannity every evening at 6 p.m. and Greta Van Susteren at 7 p.m. He listened to Rush Limbaugh in the car.

But then, Bekki noticed her husband starting to sound different.

“I was listening to these angry guys all day,” Lindner said. “She called me out on my negativity.”

“We were both just sick of it,” Bekki said.

Eventually, the church could barely afford his salary, and the couple needed health care through the Affordable Care Act. Lindner realized that some of his values, such as accessible health care and fully funded public education, didn’t align with the people he listened to for hours a day.

Then Bekki read “Becoming,” former first lady Michelle Obama’s memoir, and they started to describe themselves as more purple than red.

“We don't really do any news at all anymore,” he said.

So as pundits discussed the rise of Christian nationalism across the country, the Lindners were tuned out.

They didn’t notice when then-Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene said in a 2022 interview, “We should be Christian nationalists.”

They didn’t follow as laws were passed in Louisiana, Texas and Arkansas requiring that the Ten Commandments be displayed in public school classrooms.

They didn’t hear when House Speaker Mike Johnson called the separation of church and state a “misnomer” or when Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) said in 2024: “Some will say I am calling America a Christian nation. And so I am. And some will say that I am advocating Christian nationalism. And so I do.”

Or when Vice President JD Vance said in 2025: “The only thing that has truly served as an anchor of the United States of America is that we have been, and by the grace of God we always will be, a Christian nation.”

Only this year did that phrase — Christian nationalism — pop up in this small town, about 30 miles from deep-blue Portland. Lindner worried that Christianity as a whole could become collateral damage.

08302026_BattleGround_053 copy.jpg (3000x4865, AR: 0.62)He understood why devout Christians would invest in their community. A verse in Jeremiah talks about seeking the peace and prosperity of the city you live in.

“Because when it flourishes,” he said, “you flourish.”

But how, he wondered, did the Bible support imposing religion on others? Was that happening here?

He had tried to embrace the uncomfortable when he joined what he viewed as an extremely liberal community on Facebook — a local chapter of Indivisible, a national progressive group. He wanted to learn why they were convinced and scared and angry.

At first, he lurked. Then:

“I’m the pastor of a small church in BG, and I know people may make assumptions about me based on that. It's okay, I'm used to it.”

The reaction was swift.

“I'm a bit weary of christian ministers who take it upon themselves to tell people how to live their lives and how to fight the battle against christian supremacy.”

He had tried to bring people together in the broader Battle Ground Facebook group of more than 40,000. He was hosting a meeting, he wrote, for anyone who wanted to “build a hopeful future."

“Then DON'T hold in a church.”

“ANTIFA outsiders trying to hijack Battle Ground city hall.”

“You may not be the best choice to lead this.”

Lindner wondered if that was true.

* * *

Over in a local park, Shila Clark, a local resident of over 20 years, pulled a few copies of a zine out of her bag.

This, she told the women sitting around the picnic table, was a guide on who was leading the Christian nationalist movement. The women leaned forward as Clark explained how all these people were connected and why they should care.

The brothers who run Maddox kept buying properties in town. Their pastor appeared on podcasts with a recognized Christian nationalist. The mayor worked for Maddox. To them, the web was clear.

She taught them their names: Camden Spiller, the CEO; Wiley, his pastor; and Doug Wilson, a pastor in Idaho who has made headlines for saying that America should become a Christian nation and that married women should lose the right to vote. (A representative for Wilson declined an interview request on his behalf.)

And Clark referenced a years-old speech Wiley gave where he said Presbyterians bring “the resources of a public theology that helps us to govern unbelievers.”

More recently, a host on Steve Bannon’s far-right podcast “War Room” called Wiley “one of the leading thinkers in Christian nationalism.” Wiley did not correct him.

The women at the park flipped through the zine.

“The brothers have snuck up on us,” said Shari Kotzen Shelton, a 64-year-old health care analyst.
08302026_BattleGround_020 copy.jpg (3000x2400, AR: 1.25)That big party, Clark reminded them, the one with fireworks and a bounce house? Maddox sponsored it.

“My kid went to that Fourth of July party!” said Sheila Weitzel, a retiree who lives in the county. “There were free hot dogs and free stuff. They said it was great.”

Clark pushed back. At first, Clark said, she’d been happy to see Maddox invest in the community. But not anymore.

“They want to buy third spaces so they have control,” she said. “They’re like a cancer that is already spreading.”

As far as the accusations of Christian nationalism, Camden Spiller wrote in an email to The Washington Sun: “I’m not sure what that term means, but more often than not, it seems to be an ambiguous pejorative or scare-label used to marginalize people of faith as extremists. It’s not a label with which I identify.”

Spiller had already taken to the local newspaper in March to defend himself in a 2,000-word commentary explaining that his family simply wanted to invest in their hometown. His wife’s family is from Clark County, making their children the sixth generation to grow up here.

“As someone who is sincere about my Christian faith, I believe my faith calls me to use the gifts and opportunities God has given for His glory and our neighbors’ good,” his email to The Sun said. “If you’re trying to bring race into it, I’m proud of my Mexican and American heritage. If you’re trying to bring politics into it, my politics are centered on bringing local businesses and vibrancy to our Main Street in a way that elevates the quality of life for everyone in this community.”

Max Booth, Maddox’s vice president of real estate development, told the City Council last summer that the company had invested in 30 properties. In an email to The Sun, Booth said, “People are entitled to their opinion. My focus is on running a successful company, and doing my part to make my community an even better place to live, work, and raise a family.”

The crisscross of accusations had ensnared anyone associated with Maddox, including the couple running Al & Ernie’s Bakery Cafe.

A local farm had collaborated with them over the summer, providing strawberries for shortcake. But after the farm posted a photo of the pastries inside Al & Ernie’s, the comments quickly turned.

“Hey Bi-Zi farms, so are you telling all of us that you support Christian nationalism?” one person wrote. Hours later, the farm replied: “We can verify that we are not part of a Christian nationalism church or movement.”

On a recent Tuesday morning, as customers grabbed bagels, coffee and pastries, Joylyn Bowen, who runs Al & Ernie’s with her husband, was clear: “I’m not a nationalist.”

“They're speaking about something they really don't know anything about.”
08302026_BattleGround_005 copy.jpg (3008x4869, AR: 0.62)Her family has lived in this town for four generations. Her grandfather is the namesake Ernie and her grandmother taught her how to make pie crusts.

The backs of the buzzers they hand out to people waiting for their lattes include references to Psalms, including 34:8: "Taste and see that the Lord is good.”

But, added her husband, Devin Bowen, “it's not like we make you recite a Bible verse before you get your food.”

* * *

School hadn’t started yet, so Lindner had some free time.

He sat on the purple couch in his living room that August morning, below his family photos, the “It’s a Wonderful Life” sign and the cross. He couldn’t stop thinking about the arguments across town and his faith.

He opened his laptop, pulled up Chat GPT and asked it to tell him the specific biblical arguments Doug Wilson makes to support Christian nationalism.

“Talk to me about it,” he wrote, “ask me questions, challenge me.”

“Which biblical commands may government enforce against everyone,” ChatGPT asked, “and which belong only to disciples living by the Spirit?"

Easy, Lindner thought. So much about being a Christian is devoting yourself to Jesus’ teachings in quiet moments and in your thoughts, when no one is watching.

“You cannot be forced to love God with all your heart, mind, soul and strength,” he wrote. “That requires total surrender. And you cannot love your neighbor as yourself if you have not been empowered by the Spirit to do so.”

Yes, Lindner argued, some laws do align with the Ten Commandments: Thou shalt not murder. Thou shalt not steal.

But others, he thought, are clearly different: Thou shalt not covet. Thou shalt not have any other gods before God. Thou shalt not make yourself an idol. Thou shalt not take the Lord's name in vain. Remember the Sabbath Day.

“Maybe our country and other liberal countries have moved further away from them than we would like,” he wrote. “But forcing a nonbeliever to stay married because adultery is illegal isn’t going to produce the good fruit of the Kingdom. It will produce resentment toward the Kingdom of God.”

He didn’t understand how forcing Christian ideals could ever work. It was the opposite of what he preached — God wants people to choose to open their hearts. He gave us free will.

* * *

The local Pride organizer had a coffee date with the wife of an accused Christian nationalist.

Jessica Cole had been inspired by one of Lindner’s group discussions and introduced herself to Andrea Booth, whose husband led Maddox’s real estate development. Now they were meeting up and she wasn’t sure where to sit. Outside where everyone could see them? In a corner?

Cole ordered a hibiscus lemonade. Booth got an Americano. They chose a shady spot by the grass.

Booth made it clear she was here as a resident, not a representative of Maddox. She worried whatever she said would be conflated with her husband’s company. Still, she wanted to know: “Where did we go wrong?”

“What was the turning point that all of a sudden everybody's at each other? Because it didn't used to be that way.”
08302026_BattleGround_033 copy.jpg (3000x2400, AR: 1.25)Cole understood. People made assumptions about her, too. Most didn’t realize that she used to be very religious. She homeschooled her kids and read a handful of Doug Wilson’s books on parenting and marriage.

She didn’t adhere to Wilson’s worldview anymore, but she told Booth she was frustrated by some of the people who only recently became involved in town politics. In her view, they were grandstanding instead of looking for solutions.

“What is the definition of Christian nationalism?” Cole asked.

Booth shook her head. The avalanche of criticism, she said, had prompted her to ask her husband: “They're saying we’re Christian nationalists. What is that?”

“We never use that term to identify ourselves,” she said.

For the first time, Cole said, their Pride event this year faced threats of outside agitators. Booth’s family had been yelled at and flipped off on their way to church.

This wasn’t the environment either of them wanted for their community. Booth looked out at Main Street, nestled into the hills, and said this view made her think of her childhood home in a small South Dakota town near Mount Rushmore.

Her family had small traditions here, like ending long bike rides at a local brewery for fries and a soda. Her kids called it happy hour.

“Lord willing, we want our kids to be here so we can be around our future grandchildren,” she said. “We want to provide this great community where they can bike ride and have sweet memories.”

Cole thought of when she crossed the street with her kid, who had the nonbinary flag sticking in their hat. A man drove by, she told Booth, rolled down his window and yelled “F- - - - t go home.”
08302026_BattleGround_059 copy.jpg (3000x2400, AR: 1.25)“It’s hurtful,” Booth said, her eyes welling. “As a mom, I can't imagine having anything yelled at my child.”

“All that is to say, my kids don't want to stay here,” Cole said. She took a long pause. She thought about how the mayor did not issue a supportive proclamation for Pride month this summer and how that made her kids feel unsafe.

“So, hearing your story, I love your story for your family, and I wish that was the story for my family.”

“I hope it becomes your story,” Booth said.

They talked for hours. About local politics. About homeschooling. About the kind of town they hope Battle Ground can still be. Before leaving, Booth felt she needed to clarify something, especially in a charged environment where others see them on opposing sides.

“So,” Booth said, “I have to ask because I want to respect you. If I see you at a City Council meeting …” 

Cole interrupted:

“You can say hi.”
* * *

They were starting the Book of Joshua, which begins with God telling Joshua that Moses is dead. Lindner stood before his small congregation and reminded them about the pressure Joshua must have felt to fill Moses' shoes, to assume a new role.

The future is rarely clear, he told them, but that shouldn’t stop them from trying to lead.

“We're all going to come across situations where we feel unsettled and out of place,” he said on an August Sunday. “We're all going to have problems we've never had to solve before.”

Neighbors might keep turning on each other. The truth might blur. People might lose trust in each other, their local government, their pastor. There will be questions he can’t answer.

“You don't have to see the whole story to be able to take the next step, right?” he told them. “You just can go one frame at a time.”

So on the first Thursday in September, Lindner convened a fledgling monthly effort to bring people together.
08302026_BattleGround_007 copy.jpg (3000x2400, AR: 1.25)He’d thought through what he hoped to accomplish and had written it down. “We want to become a community that can have difficult conversations without turning each other into enemies.”

He’d made a bulleted list of rules: Listen to understand. Don’t interrupt. Be curious before being certain. Be honest without being cruel.

He’d written discussion questions. He wanted this to work, to get people to talk to each other.

He printed 10 copies of the rules, grabbed a stack of name tags and finally, he was ready.

First came a friend who had advertised the event, along with her husband. Then two others who were helping him coordinate the meetings.

Thirty minutes went by. Lindner told himself it was the first week of school. People were busy. Maybe they just didn’t want to come here. He decided to ask a local restaurant to host them next month. He kept waiting.

They sat inside his church for over an hour, but no one new walked through the door.

entries.title: The Mystics Hope to Regain Their Momentum After a World Cup Break
entries.summary: Washington will play its first game in 20 days on Thursday.
entries.content:
The Mystics will return from their summer break in full force.

Washington will play its first game in 20 days on Thursday after a nearly three-week WNBA hiatus for the FIBA World Cup. The Mystics had three players participate in the tournament: Sonia Citron and Kiki Iriafen for Team USA, and Alicia Florez for Spain.

All three players were absent from practice on Monday in D.C., but Mystics coach Sydney Johnson said the trio will play without restrictions Thursday against the Chicago Sky.

“Full go, full steam ahead,” Johnson said of their status.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Prior to the break, the Mystics had won five of their last seven games, clinching their first playoff berth since 2023. With four regular season games remaining, the team sits seventh in the WNBA standings.

While the team was playing well before the hiatus, Johnson and his players agreed that a break was welcome. Rookie center Lauren Betts told The Sun that she and the other seven rookies on the team have been playing basketball for “a year straight” because they were drafted shortly after their final college seasons ended.

Betts and fellow rookie Angela Dugalic had the longest college season possible after winning the national championship at UCLA.

“I really needed a break mentally and physically from basketball,” Betts said. “So I did a lot of lifting on my own, but as far as basketball, I really tried to stay away from it for a week so I can come back and just be excited to be back and refreshed. I feel like it was really helpful.”

Mystics forward Michaela Onyenwere split her break between Los Angeles and Hawaii, staying up as late as 2 a.m. to watch her teammates play in Berlin. She compared the hiatus to an Olympic break, which she had during her rookie season in 2024. She said that Johnson’s message to the team has been “just because we took a break off doesn’t mean our identity waivers.”

“[Hoping to] to pick up where we left off,” Onyenwere said. “Last game [before the break] was kind of disappointing for us but we want to hone in on the things we were doing well — playing in transition, being a really great defensive unit.”

Citron and Iriafen were both late additions to Team USA’s roster after Kelsey Plum and A’ja Wilson dropped out for health reasons. Neither Mystics player carved out a large role for Team USA in Berlin, averaging roughly 11 minutes per game during the Americans’ gold medal run. Florez played about the same number of minutes for Spain.

Johnson said he wasn’t concerned about his players after their time in Berlin and is confident his team can maintain momentum after the long layoff.

“I think it's disrupted everybody’s momentum,” Johnson said. “I think we’re equally advantaged and disadvantaged. So I don't want to overthink it. I think for us as much as anything is trying to get the rust off a little bit and trying to get back into our groove. I think everybody’s gonna have to deal with that.”

entries.title: Trump Rages After the Supreme Court Halted His Mail-in Ballot Order
entries.summary: The president referred to the justices as “merely a shell of their original selves,” in a post criticizing their Monday decision.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump wrote a scathing criticism of the Supreme Court on Tuesday, condemning its Monday decision to stop the U.S. Postal Service from implementing a rule that would change the mail-in voting process nationwide.

“Republicans just got another bad decision from the United States Supreme Court, one that the Court System took forever to give, and then blamed it, in part, on no time left to implement a solution to our totally CORRUPT and out of control Mail-In voting ‘disaster,’ which is a laughing stock all over the World,” the president wrote on Truth Social.

Monday’s decision to halt the final rule, which was based on a March executive order from Trump, is yet another loss for the president as he attempts to tighten restrictions on voting before the midterms.

The final rule would have required states to overhaul their mail-in voting systems on a tight deadline that would have cost money, time and resources that many election officials argued they did not have. It would also require the USPS to roll out an untested portal to collect the personal information of all eligible voters, although postal officials who spoke with The Washington Sun and a whistleblower emphasized that the system would not be ready in time for the midterms.

The Supreme Court has six Republican appointees, half of whom were appointed by Trump himself. Only justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented on Monday, while the remainder of the high court ruled in favor of halting the final rule less than two months before the midterm elections.

“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court,” Trump wrote. “They are merely a shell of their original selves, a Court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won’t be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal.”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in his decision, “There is at least a fair prospect that

the final rule falls within the Postal Service’s statutory authority.” While Kavanaugh did agree that there was not enough time before the midterms, there is still a chance that the Supreme Court may allow Trump to implement the changes before the 2028 election.

Trump acknowledged that his criticism of the court, which included its other decisions against the president on birthright citizenship and tariffs, “will likely cost me dearly for years to come.”
entries.author: Adora Brown

entries.title: Mike Rogers to Skip Michigan Senate Debate Over Beef With Local News Anchor
entries.summary: Mike Rogers’ campaign accused the moderator of showing bias for Abdul El-Sayed, who has challenged the former representative to five debates.
entries.content:
Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers will not attend a debate held by a local television station Tuesday over suspicions that the event’s moderator has “bias and favoritism” toward his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, Rogers’ campaign said in a news release.

The campaign listed several allegations that Roop Raj, an anchor at Fox 2 Detroit with experience interviewing high-profile political candidates, has conducted himself “in a manner that is inconsistent with the level of gravity required to moderate a debate for the number one U.S. Senate race in the country.”

El-Sayed has challenged Rogers to debate him five times prior to the November midterm elections. Rogers, whose race is considered a “toss up” by the Cook Political Report, has so far agreed to two debates scheduled for Oct. 8 and Oct. 21 on separate networks.

The Fox 2 Detroit debate will proceed Tuesday featuring El-Sayed and a podium left open for Rogers, the station said, adding that the “invitation still stands.”

Rogers’ campaign criticized Raj on several fronts, including his handling of a Republican gubernatorial primary debate where three political insiders asked questions, the fact that he has been praised by leftist internet personality Hasan Piker and for remarks he made on Aug. 24 where he called Rogers a “veteran politician” and El-Sayed an “outsider who is pretty brilliant in many ways, whether you like him or not.”

“Michiganders deserve to see their candidates engage in a healthy, fair debate — not one compromised by media bias,” Rogers campaign spokesperson Alyssa Brouillet said in a statement.

Raj did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Rogers’ accusations.

Raj and the Michigan Debate Commission have in recent weeks directly petitioned Rogers to attend a debate with El-Sayed on Fox 2 Detroit. Raj wrote in a social post on X that candidates for office “need to show up for debates,” adding, “Curating social media ads and then appearing on network cable channels of their political leaning for easy interviews does nothing for the electorate back here in Michigan.”

Raj also addressed the criticism levied toward him on Monday, saying he and Rogers have had a “very good, fair and productive conversation on many occasions.”

“I respect his experience and leadership,” Raj wrote on X. “I hope he is able to make time for this debate. I’ll do my job with integrity and responsibility as I always strive to do. I certainly hope you will do the same when messaging here.”

entries.title: Capitals Star Alex Ovechkin Appears in Pro-Putin Campaign Video
entries.summary: Celebrity chef and Caps fan José Andrés expressed his opposition on social media, calling it a “sad day” for the team.
entries.content:
Capitals star Alex Ovechkin appeared Monday in a campaign ad for the United Russia party in support of its leader, President Vladimir Putin, ahead of the country’s parliamentary elections that are set to run Friday to Sunday.

The 40-year-old team captain was in images published by Vedomosti, a Russian newspaper, alongside other pro-Putin figures including Russia’s foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov. He also appeared in a video alongside Lavrov and other Russian celebrities such as actor Vladimir Mashkov.

Ovechkin and Putin have a longstanding relationship. In 2017, The Washington Post reported that Ovechkin had a personal phone number for Putin and received a gift from him at his wedding the same year. A year later, Ovechkin started PutinTeam, a social movement to support Putin ahead of the 2018 Russian presidential election.

“I'm not a politic,” Ovechkin told the Post in 2017. “I don't know what's happening out there. I know it's a hard situation, but it is what it is. You know, I play here, and this is my second home. I don't want to fight between two countries, because it's going to be a mess.”

After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Ovechkin altered his tone and wished for peace without condemning Putin.

“Obviously, it's a hard situation,” Ovechkin said shortly after the invasion. “I have lots of friends in Russia and Ukraine, and it's hard to see the war. I hope soon it's going to be over and there's going to be peace in the whole world.”

In response to seeing Ovechkin appear in a pro-Putin ad, celebrity chef and Capitals fan José Andrés reposted on X and said, “Russia is killing Americans in the Middle East with drones that help Iran! @Capitals @NHL @ovi8 and what Russians are doing in Ukraine is wrong…..killing civilians everyday….sad day for my beloved DC team!!”

The NHL and the Capitals did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Ovechkin, who is entering what could be his final season, has been with the organization since 2004, when he was the No. 1 pick in the NHL draft. He led the Capitals to the 2018 Stanley Cup and broke Wayne Gretzky’s all-time NHL scoring record in 2025. He signed a one-year contract extension with the Capitals in July.

entries.title: The Washington Sun partners with Capital Weather to deliver trusted, local weather coverage
entries.summary: The Washington Sun will enter an exclusive licensing agreement with Capital Weather to share daily forecasts.
entries.content:
The Washington Sun announced today an exclusive licensing agreement with Capital Weather, the D.C. region’s most credible and reliable source for weather coverage.

Capital Weather started as an independent website in 2004, partnered with The Washington Post starting in 2008, and became independent again in 2026.

As part of this new partnership, The Washington Sun will be the only news organization to host its daily forecast, updated multiple times throughout the day.

“People who live and work in Washington, D.C., deserve weather information they can trust, delivered by people who deeply understand our commitment to keeping our community informed and safe,” said The Washington Sun’s CEO, Arielle Elliott. “We’re thrilled to have the expertise of Capital Weather and their extensive track record of accuracy and trust featured on The Washington Sun.”

“We’re excited to partner with The Washington Sun to expand the reach of our local forecast across the D.C. region,” said Capital Weather founder and chief meteorologist Jason Samenow. “This partnership is another way for us to help more Washingtonians plan their day and stay safe.”

Capital Weather’s forecasts will be available on washingtonsun.com/weather.

For press inquiries about The Washington Sun, email communications manager Thuy Lan Nguyen at thuylannguyen@washingtonsun.com.
